tldr: The Pile is an 825.18 GiB English pretraining corpus assembled from 22 diverse, curated sources — spanning academic writing, code, legal text, prose, and dialogue — and trains significantly better language models than Common Crawl alone.
overview: EleutherAI's Pile combines 14 newly introduced datasets with 8 existing ones to produce a 825.18 GiB corpus (1,254.20 GiB effective after upsampling) designed specifically to improve cross-domain generalisation for large language models. Each constituent dataset was chosen for domain diversity and quality: sources range from PubMed Central and ArXiv to GitHub, FreeLaw, Stack Exchange, and fiction books. Component weights are tuned so that higher-quality sources (e.g. Wikipedia at 3 epochs, Books3 at 1.5 epochs) appear more often per training epoch than lower-quality ones. Empirically, 1.3B-parameter models trained on the Pile outperform CC-100 and raw Common Crawl models on every Pile component and on standard benchmarks, with the largest gains on academic, code, and mathematical datasets.

sections.title: Abstract & 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates the Pile by arguing that dataset diversity improves downstream generalisation. Introduces the 825.18 GiB corpus of 22 subsets, notes that GPT-2 and GPT-3 struggle on many Pile components (especially academic writing), and lists four core contributions: the dataset, 14 new sub-datasets, evaluation results, and thorough documentation.

sections.title: 1.1 Contributions
sections.summary: Four explicit contributions: (1) the 825.18 GiB corpus combining 22 sources; (2) 14 newly introduced language-modeling datasets; (3) evaluations showing significant BPB improvement over CC-100 on all components; (4) an in-depth investigation and documentation intended to help researchers make informed decisions.

sections.title: 2. The Pile Datasets
sections.summary: Describes all 22 components in detail. The five largest by effective size are Pile-CC (227.12 GiB, 18.11%), PubMed Central (180.55 GiB, 14.40%), Books3 (151.44 GiB, 12.07%), OpenWebText2 (125.54 GiB, 10.01%), and ArXiv (112.42 GiB, 8.96%). Each sub-dataset's raw size, sampling weight, epoch count, effective size, and mean document size are given in Table 1. Newly introduced sources include Pile-CC, PubMed Central, OpenWebText2, GitHub, FreeLaw, Stack Exchange, USPTO Backgrounds, PubMed Abstracts, Ubuntu IRC, BookCorpus2, HackerNews, YouTube Subtitles, PhilPapers, and NIH ExPorter.

sections.title: 3. Benchmarking Language Models with the Pile
sections.summary: Proposes bits-per-UTF-8-byte (BPB) as the evaluation metric (invariant to tokenisation differences) and describes train/validation/test splits (0.1% each for val and test, totalling over 1 GiB each). Reports zero-shot perplexity for GPT-2 (four sizes) and GPT-3 (four sizes) on each Pile component; GPT-3 davinci achieves the best BPB on most components but scores poorly on academic writing, code, DM Mathematics, and FreeLaw — domains underrepresented in its web-based training data.

sections.title: 4. Evaluation
sections.summary: Trains 1.3B-parameter GPT-2-architecture models from scratch on the Pile, CC-100 (en), and raw Common Crawl, each subsampled to 40 GiB for a fair size-controlled comparison. The Pile model achieves the best BPB on all 22 held-out component sets and improves WikiText perplexity, while CC-100 wins on LAMBADA accuracy — likely because CC-100's Wikipedia-biased perplexity filter removes the diversity that makes Pile broadly better.

sections.title: 5. Structural Statistics
sections.summary: Examines document-length distributions (most documents are short with a long tail past 60,000 bytes) and mean bytes-per-GPT-2-token per component. Sources like NIH ExPorter and OpenWebText2 are syntactically close to WebText (high bytes/token), while GitHub, ArXiv, DM Mathematics, and EuroParl show the lowest bytes/token, indicating structural divergence from typical web text. Pile is 97.4% English by fasttext classification.

sections.title: 6. Investigating and Documenting the Datasets
sections.summary: Provides documentation via datasheets and data statements. Conducts LDA topic modeling (16 topics on each component) and evaluates topical divergence from Pile-CC; EuroParl, Enron Emails, and Ubuntu IRC diverge most. Analyses profanity rates per component (Pile as a whole is less profane than Pile-CC alone) and performs co-occurrence bias analysis for gender, religion, and race, documenting skews while explicitly choosing to document rather than eliminate problematic content.

sections.title: 7. Implications and Broader Impacts
sections.summary: Addresses legality (arguing fair-use under US copyright law given non-commercial, transformative use), author consent (three-tier framework: public data, ToS-compliant data, authorial-consent data), acceleration of AI timelines, and risks from misaligned language models. Concludes that thorough documentation is the best available response, as directly filtering undesirable content from training data is unlikely to prevent harmful outputs.

sections.title: 8. Related Work
sections.summary: Situates the Pile relative to Wikipedia+BookCorpus (GPT/BERT), the Common Crawl family (C4/mC4, CC-100, raw CC), and GPT-3's curated mix. Notes that all prior large-scale alternatives are derived predominantly from Common Crawl, whereas the Pile deliberately combines web scrapes with smaller, higher-quality targeted datasets — a design principle the paper argues is essential as models scale.

readingFocus: How component weights and epoch counts (Table 1) translate raw dataset sizes into effective training-data proportions — directly relevant to designing Phase 1 data mixing for Microlab.
The BPB metric and per-component evaluation methodology: understand why computing perplexity per-document rather than over a concatenated corpus matters for cross-domain benchmarking.
Why a diversity-first corpus (the Pile) outperforms a quality-filtered single-source corpus (CC-100) across nearly every domain — the core argument for curated multi-source pretraining.

The three-tier consent framework (public / ToS-compliant / authorial consent) and the bias-documentation methodology: useful context when deciding which data sources to include or exclude in Microlab's own training corpus.
GPT-3's per-component weaknesses (academic writing, code, legal text, DM Mathematics) as a guide to which domains are most underrepresented in web-only corpora and therefore most valuable to add.
